title: Disagreements in analyses of rhetorical text structure: A new dataset and first analyses
venue: Proceedings of the 19th Linguistic Annotation Workshop (LAW-XIX-2025)
task_description: Evaluate and inspect legitimate disagreement by retaining two parallel Rhetorical Structure Theory analyses for each text and enumerating conflicting decisions.
inputs: English and German texts; text segments; two independent analyses by trained annotators.
outputs_or_labels: Two alternative RST discourse trees; conflict-decision list; disagreement statistics and qualitative ambiguity typology.
pipeline_gap_filled: alternative valid parses and disagreement-aware evaluation of discourse/argument structure
artifact_access_status: ACL landing page and PDF accessible; dataset artifact link not confirmed in retained evidence
license_status: Not stated in retained evidence; do not infer from ACL access
evidence_basis: ACL abstract/PDF explicitly defines legitimate disagreement as multiple valid annotations, gives parallel English/German analyses, and distinguishes linguistic ambiguity from scheme/specification ambiguity.
limitations: RST discourse relations are not argumentation labels; the retained page did not expose a stable downloadable dataset URL.
why_relevant: Closest direct precedent for scoring a system against a set of defensible discourse structures rather than one gold tree; relation and nuclearity alternatives can preserve multiple argument interpretations.

title: Disagreement Space in Argument Analysis
authors: Annette Hautli-Janisz; Ella Schad; Chris Reed
venue: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Perspectivist Approaches to NLP @ LREC2022
task_description: Retain non-aggregated argument annotations and classify disagreement causes across argument segmentation, relation, and graph-analysis decisions.
inputs: 67 excerpts of BBC Question Time political debate; 150–250 words each; two independent annotators; full IAT graphs.
outputs_or_labels: 134 argument graphs; 1,817 propositions; 1,402 disagreement labels categorized as errors, fuzziness, or ambiguity, including AMB-REL and AMB-SPLIT.
pipeline_gap_filled: alternative valid argument graphs; disagreement-preserving argument interpretation
artifact_access_status: ACL PDF accessible; paper says resource will be openly available, but a separate current download URL was not verified
evidence_basis: ACL/PDF evidence reports 67 excerpts, 134 graphs, 1,817 propositions, and explicit ambiguity/fuzziness/error categories; search evidence reports 207 ambiguity labels.
limitations: The corpus includes annotation errors alongside legitimate ambiguity, so filtering/weighting is required; artifact availability beyond paper is uncertain.
why_relevant: Best direct argument-mining resource for preserving multiple graph interpretations and distinguishing ambiguity from annotator error instead of collapsing to a single gold graph.

title: We're Afraid Language Models Aren't Modeling Ambiguity
authors: Alisa Liu; Zhaofeng Wu; Julian Michael; Alane Suhr; Peter West; Alexander Koller; Swabha Swayamdipta; Noah A. Smith; Yejin Choi
task_description: Recognize and represent ambiguity in natural-language inference by allowing multiple entailment labels and providing a disambiguating rewrite for each valid interpretation.
inputs: 1,645 English premise–hypothesis examples covering lexical, syntactic, and pragmatic ambiguity; curated and generated/filtered examples.
outputs_or_labels: Single or multiple NLI labels; ambiguous cases have label-specific disambiguating rewrites; multilabel NLI evaluation and ambiguity recognition.
pipeline_gap_filled: multi-label logical interpretations and explicit alternative readings for claim/argument semantics
artifact_access_status: Official GitHub repository exposes data, annotations, preprocessing, evaluation, and training code
license_status: CC BY 4.0 stated in official repository README
evidence_basis: ACL/PDF search evidence states 1,645 examples, 35.2% multi-label ambiguous examples, and disambiguating rewrites; official GitHub confirms data/annotations and multilabel evaluation code.
limitations: NLI labels are entailment relations rather than argument components or discourse graphs; generated examples and rewrites require provenance checks when reused.
why_relevant: A reusable mechanism for representing an argument claim under several valid readings before relation/strength evaluation; directly supports set-valued labels and interpretation-conditioned scoring.

title: Would you describe a leopard as yellow? Evaluating crowd-annotations with justified and informative disagreement
authors: Pia Sommerauer; Antske Fokkens; Piek Vossen
venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computational Linguistics (COLING 2020)
benchmark_or_resource_name: SPT diagnostic semantic-property annotation with justified disagreement
task_description: Evaluate semantic judgments while distinguishing justified disagreement caused by ambiguity/vagueness from annotation noise, using multiple worker judgments and expert validation.
inputs: Property–concept descriptions; ten crowd annotations per item; semantic relations designed to elicit positive/negative/graded judgments.
outputs_or_labels: Per-item annotation distributions, expert annotations, worker consistency/quality signals, and disagreement-quality metrics rather than only majority labels.
pipeline_gap_filled: disagreement-aware evaluation and ambiguity/noise separation for proposition interpretation
artifact_access_status: ACL PDF and official GitHub artifact accessible
license_status: License not verified in retained evidence
evidence_basis: ACL/PDF evidence describes expected disagreement, ten workers per unit, and goals of separating justified disagreement from noise; repository URL is given in the paper.
limitations: Not argument-specific and not a parse/tree benchmark; semantic-property descriptions are synthetic/diagnostic rather than authentic debates.
why_relevant: Provides an operational evaluation pattern for preserving annotator distributions and testing whether disagreement is meaningful before collapsing interpretations into a gold label.

title: Benchmarking Meaning Representations in Neural Semantic Parsing
authors: Jiaqi Guo; Qian Liu; Jian-Guang Lou; Zhenwen Li; Xueqing Liu; Tao Xie; Ting Liu
task_description: Compare semantic parsers across multiple meaning representations while evaluating both exact-match and execution-match equivalence.
inputs: Natural-language utterances from Geo, ATIS, and Jobs; four meaning representations including Prolog, Lambda Calculus, FunQL, and SQL.
outputs_or_labels: Annotated logical forms in four representations; execution engines; exact-match and execution-match scores; manually checked translations/executions.
pipeline_gap_filled: alternative logical forms and semantics-preserving evaluation of structured interpretations
artifact_access_status: ACL landing page/PDF and Microsoft Research description accessible; source-code/data repository not independently verified
evidence_basis: ACL/PDF and Microsoft Research evidence describe three datasets × four meaning representations, six execution engines, completed logical forms, and execution-match evaluation for semantically equivalent forms.
limitations: Alternative meaning representations are schema translations, not independent human parses; task-oriented utterances are not argument texts.
why_relevant: Strong control for evaluating semantic equivalence rather than surface-form identity, useful when multiple argument skeletons realize the same logical content.

title: From Disagreement to Understanding: The Case for Ambiguity Detection in NLI
venue: Proceedings of the 5th Workshop on Perspectivist Approaches to NLP
task_description: Detect and classify ambiguity in premise–hypothesis pairs before performing inference, treating disagreement as a signal of divergent valid interpretations.
inputs: NLI premise–hypothesis pairs with ambiguous premise/hypothesis phenomena and annotation disagreement.
outputs_or_labels: Ambiguity categories, ambiguity detection/classification stage, and interpretation-conditioned inference proposal; no released benchmark artifact verified.
pipeline_gap_filled: disagreement-aware interpretation before argument relation/strength scoring
artifact_access_status: ACL landing page/PDF accessible; no separate dataset/repository artifact verified
evidence_basis: ACL abstract explicitly proposes ambiguity detection/classification before inference and a unified taxonomy of ambiguity subtypes tied to disagreement.
limitations: Position paper/framework rather than a released benchmark; no artifact access confirmed in retained evidence.
why_relevant: Useful design specification for a benchmark that reports ambiguity detection separately from downstream entailment/contradiction or argument-strength decisions.
